records.title: Cosmic Records — Catalogue History
records.summary: Cosmic Records brings together COSMIC 001–017 as one body of work in Justin Scott Dixon’s portfolio, centered on DJ’s Friction & Spice and Voyager. Label owners and producers: Justin Scott Dixon (DJ Friction / Voyager) and Jeff Alderson (DJ Spice). Other artist identities and contributions are documented within the relevant releases.

items.title: Emotional continuity

records.title: Studio evolution
records.summary: Dixon’s account connects changes in instruments, sequencing, mixing and monitoring with changes in the music he could make.

gallery.caption: Original artwork awaiting source reconciliation.

sections.title: Before Cosmic: listening, performance and editing
sections.intro: Dixon recalls these formative experiences in his Super Progressive interview; exact dates remain unstated.

items.title: Learning to listen
items.detail: Family stereo equipment and a fascination with the DJ booth connected music, sound systems and performance long before the Cosmic recordings.

items.title: Programming a night
items.detail: Early club work developed his sense of continuity and musical pacing. Radio production introduced reel-to-reel tape editing as a way to rearrange music.

items.title: From systems to songs
items.detail: Sound and lighting work, followed by computer sequencing and sampling, formed the bridge into the studio and the Friction & Spice partnership with Jeff Alderson.

items.title: Merritt Island
items.detail: External samplers and synthesizers, a DOS sequencer and a compact console formed the early Cosmic studio.

items.title: Effects as arrangement
items.detail: Dixon describes carefully programmed delays and selected reverbs as central to the spatial character of those records.

items.title: Larger consoles
items.detail: After COSMIC 009, the Mackie 24-8 and expanded MIDI routing gave him more room to visualize and organize arrangements.

items.title: Time Travel
items.detail: Logic sequencing and the Yamaha 03D changed the workflow. Digital mixing and mastering introduced new lessons in headroom, synchronization and loudness.

items.title: Aria — One
items.detail: The 2001 remix represents tighter rhythmic alignment, expanded sampling and local effects processing in Dixon’s account.

items.title: Logic instruments
items.detail: EXS24, Absynth, ES2, EVOC and later software tools expanded his cinematic palette and reduced the effort of recalling sessions.

sections.title: AK1200: capturing the performance
sections.intro: Artist-recalled recording sessions. Album-edition credits and session dates remain to be verified.

items.title: Recording engineering and corrective editing
items.detail: Dixon provided the recording environment and captured AK1200 performing vinyl DJ sets. Where needed, he joined passages from restarted takes to repair performance errors.

items.title: The performer and the engineer
items.detail: AK1200 selected and performed the music. Dixon’s contribution was capture and editing before delivery to the label for subsequent mastering.

items.title: A practical digital workflow
items.detail: He recalls capturing and editing the performance in Pro Tools, with separate booth and studio monitoring, then delivering the files on a data CD.

items.title: Almost Flew
items.detail: Dixon identifies this remix as a decisive application of scales to vocal placement and newly written melodies.

items.title: Pulse
items.detail: A cinematic opening leads into a heavier dance-floor section, demonstrating the compositional control he wanted to express.

items.title: Preservation
items.detail: Returning to archived hardware patches was rewarding, but also reminded him why recall and practical workflow mattered.

records.title: QVibe & immersive composition
records.summary: Contemplative pieces developed for looping visuals became source material for later immersive work. This account describes musical intentions, not therapeutic outcomes.

gallery.caption: Original artwork awaiting source reconciliation.

items.title: The brief
items.detail: Build music to accompany frequency-themed looping fractal visuals.

items.title: Tuning experiments
items.detail: Dixon recalls manually tuning instruments around target tones, with a low-level sine-wave reference throughout each piece.

items.title: Breathing space
items.detail: Long drones, sustaining piano chords and carefully paced openings and endings let the music breathe.

items.title: Anxiety
items.detail: Dixon selects this dark, textural piece as his leading immersive example. The Atmos version is artist-reported mastered and unpublished.

items.title: A stable foundation
items.detail: He retained anchored source sounds and placed accompanying effects around the listener, considering stereo and binaural translation throughout.

items.title: Calibrated monitoring
items.detail: Balancing bass management, LFE and the monitoring system made translation and dynamics central to the workflow.

publicSources.label: Artist reference playlist
publicSources.supports: Related listening references; not a verified original QVibe sequence

records.title: AI in creative practice
records.summary: AI extends Dixon’s creative range across music, visual storytelling and tool development. His listening, direction and editing shape the result.

gallery.caption: Original artwork awaiting source reconciliation.

items.title: Direction
items.detail: Story requirements, film frames and Dixon’s own musical archive guided score development.

items.title: Emotional continuity
items.detail: He selected music to establish the opening’s tone and carry the audience between tension and vulnerability.

items.title: Editorial craft
items.detail: Generated cues still required selection and editing to picture. This was a central part of his contribution.

items.title: Music exploration
items.detail: Suno experiments connect source material, stylistic direction and iterative selection.

items.title: Visual storytelling
items.detail: PROXIMITY planning uses character references, narrative continuity and storyboard packages for cross-model production.

items.title: Everyday language
items.detail: Dixon sought writing assistance that improved clarity while preserving his tone and avoiding added context.

items.title: Sound ReFormer
items.detail: A production problem—reconstructing generated material as editable performance—became an instrument-design investigation.

items.title: Repeatable methods
items.detail: His history documents prompt structures, evidence gathering and tools designed to make experiments easier to review and repeat.

items.title: Human direction
items.detail: Dixon sees the opportunity as greater expressive precision, guided by the artist’s experience and judgment.
